name: Doğu Express
desc: Twenty-four hours of railway from Ankara to Kars, climbing through the Euphrates gorges at Kemah and across the snowbound plateau at dawn. The sleeper compartments are small and the samovar at the end of the carriage is the social centre. The last hours into Kars, past frozen villages, are what people book it for.
season: Dec–Feb for the snow the trip is famous for; Jun–Sep is greener and far easier to book
tip: Book the ordinary Doğu Ekspresi rather than the pricier Turistik version — same route, a fraction of the fare, and tickets open exactly 15 days ahead on the TCDD site.
rev: Riders describe the winter run as unforgettable, while flagging chronic delays of several hours, cold or overheated carriages depending on luck, and a booking window that sells out in minutes.
onward: Board at Ankara, Kayseri, Sivas or Erzurum; Kars station is a 10-minute walk from the centre

name: Kars Kaşarı and Highland Honey
desc: Swiss cheesemakers came here in the 19th century and the technique stuck: hard aged kaşar and wheel gruyère made from cows grazing flower meadows at 2,000 m. The dairy village of Boğatepe still runs a working cellar you can walk into, and the same meadows produce dark comb honey sold straight from the frame.
season: Jun–Sep for the meadows and fresh production; cheese cellars are open year-round
tip: Drive to Boğatepe rather than buying on Kars high street — the village cooperative runs a small cheese museum and lets you taste from the ageing cellar.
todo: Buy comb honey by the frame
rev: Food travellers rate the cellar visits highly, but warn that roadside stalls sell industrial cheese under the Kars name and that the village road is rough and unlit after dark.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then 45 km northeast towards Susuz; you need a car to reach Boğatepe

name: Şeytan Castle
desc: A ruined Urartian-founded fortress balanced on a rock spur above the Karaçay gorge, reached by a footbridge over a drop that makes the name feel earned. The walls follow the cliff edge with nothing between you and the canyon. From the far towers you look down on green ravines and, on a clear day, towards Çıldır.
season: Jun–Sep; the approach path is ice or mud outside those months
tip: Wear proper shoes and keep well back from the unfenced edges — the last section is bare rock and there is no railing anywhere on the site.
rev: Visitors call it the most dramatically sited castle in the northeast, while repeatedly flagging the unprotected drops, the absence of any facilities, and a gravel access track that punishes ordinary cars.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then about 60 km north via Çıldır; combine it with the lake in one loop

name: Ilgar Pass
desc: The road from Ardahan to Posof climbs to about 2,540 m over a bare grass saddle where the weather changes in minutes and the horizon is nothing but rolling steppe and cattle. Descending north the land flips abruptly into dense spruce forest and deep valleys — one pass, two different countries' worth of landscape.
season: Jun–Sep; snow gates close it or reduce it to one lane from November to April
tip: Check the pass status before committing — it is one of the first roads in the country to be shut by drifting snow, and there is no fuel between Ardahan and Posof.
todo: Watch the forest begin on the north side
Yayla tea from a roadside hut
rev: Drivers describe the crossing as one of the emptiest and most beautiful in Türkiye, while warning about sudden fog, free-roaming cattle on the tarmac and long stretches without phone signal.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then Ardahan and north on the D010 towards Posof and the Georgian border

name: Posof
desc: The last valley before Georgia, wet enough to grow proper spruce forest and wooden houses with shingled roofs — closer to the Black Sea than to the dry plateau an hour south. Mist sits in the side valleys most mornings, the Türkgözü border gate is ten minutes away, and hardly any traveller stops on the way through.
season: Jun–Oct; heavy snow and low cloud from November
tip: Take the forest road up to Kolköy for the view back over the whole valley — the main road through town shows you almost none of it.
todo: Look across to the Georgian border
rev: The few reports call it green, silent and completely untouristed, but also note there is essentially no accommodation, one or two restaurants, and long waits for the border-bound minibus.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then Ardahan and over the Ilgar Pass; buses to the Türkgözü border gate pass through

name: Damal
desc: For about twenty minutes on summer evenings the sun throws a shadow across the Karadağ ridge above this village that reads unmistakably as Atatürk in profile, hat and all. Villagers set out chairs and watch it happen. The rest of the year Damal is quiet upland pasture with wooden barns and horses on the slopes.
season: 15 Jun–15 Sep only — the shadow needs that sun angle and a cloudless evening
tip: Be in place by about 17:30 and accept that one cloud on the ridge cancels the whole thing; there is no second showing that day.
rev: People who catch it find the effect genuinely startling; the common complaints are the crowd of coaches on peak August evenings, dust in the viewing field, and turning up on the wrong date or a cloudy night.
onward: Kars (KSY) airport, then Ardahan and about 45 km north; local buses run to Damal in summer

name: Tuzluca Salt Caves
desc: Galleries cut by hand into a hill of rock salt, worked since antiquity and still producing. The walls are grey and glassy, the air is dry and about 12 °C all year, and one chamber has been fitted out with beds for asthma treatment. Outside, blocks of salt sit stacked in the sun beside the road to Iğdır.
season: Year-round; the constant cave temperature makes it a good July escape
tip: Bring a fleece even in August and ask at the entrance whether the working gallery is open — the therapy chamber alone is a fraction of the experience.
rev: Visitors find the tunnels genuinely unusual and cheap to enter, but reviews mention poor lighting, no guiding in English, and an approach through an active quarry that feels industrial rather than scenic.
onward: Iğdır (IGD) airport, then 40 km west on the Kars road; Kars–Iğdır buses stop in Tuzluca

name: Iğdır Plain and the Ararat Face
tr: Iğdır Ovası ve Ağrı Dağı Manzarası
desc: Iğdır sits at 850 m in a warm hollow of cotton and apricot orchards, and from its northern edge Ararat rises in one uninterrupted sweep of nearly 4,300 m — the biggest single view of the mountain anywhere, better than the postcard angle from Doğubayazıt. The Aras river and the Armenian border run just beyond the fields.
season: Apr–Jun for blossom and snow on the cone; Jul–Aug is dusty and over 35 °C
tip: Drive the Aralık road at first light — the north face catches the sun while the plain is still in shadow, and the haze that ruins midday shots has not built up.
todo: North face view from the Aralık road
rev: Photographers rate the unobstructed north face highly, but visitors say the town itself has little to hold you, summer haze often hides the summit entirely, and border-zone roads mean occasional checkpoints.
onward: Iğdır (IGD) airport just outside town, or 3 hours by road from Kars over the Kağızman pass

name: Mount Ararat
desc: Türkiye's highest mountain at 5,137 m, a lone snow-capped volcano standing over 4,000 m above the plain with no rivals near it. The standard south route from Eli village is a walk-up on scree and then glacier, done over three or four days from camps at 3,200 m and 4,200 m. The summit ice cap is flat and wind-scoured.
season: Jul–Sep for the climb; the mountain is visible year-round when haze allows
tip: You cannot climb it independently — a permit through a licensed agency is mandatory and takes weeks, so arrange it long before you fly.
todo: Permit trek to the summit ice cap
Sunrise on the north face from Iğdır
rev: Climbers describe a non-technical but genuinely brutal altitude slog, and complain about permit bureaucracy, agencies of very mixed quality, rubbish at the camps and periodic closures at short notice.
onward: Iğdır (IGD) or Ağrı (AJI) airport, then to Doğubayazıt; agencies transfer you to the Eli trailhead

name: Ishak Pasha Palace
desc: An 18th-century Kurdish governor's palace on a rock terrace above Doğubayazıt, mixing Seljuk, Georgian, Armenian and Ottoman detail in one honey-coloured building. It had underfloor heating, its own mosque and a harem court with a fluted dome. Behind it a ruined citadel and a cave mosque climb the cliff, with Ararat filling the horizon.
season: Apr–Oct; the glass roof makes summer midday hot, and the road ices in winter
tip: Come in the last hour before closing — the low sun turns the stone orange and the tour buses from Van have already left.
todo: Climb to the old citadel above
rev: Almost everyone rates the setting and the carving, but the modern glass-and-steel roof added over the ruins is widely disliked, and several mention aggressive souvenir sellers in the car park.
onward: Iğdır (IGD) or Ağrı (AJI) airport, then Doğubayazıt; the palace is 6 km up a steep side road, taxi or dolmuş

name: Doğubayazıt Meteor Crater
desc: A 35 m-wide pit in bare ground a few kilometres from the Iranian border, fenced and signed as the world's second-largest meteorite crater — a claim geologists dispute. It takes five minutes to see. What makes the detour worth it is the surrounding country: military-flat steppe, Ararat behind you, and the Durupınar boat-shaped formation nearby.
season: Apr–Oct; the side road is exposed and drifts shut in winter
tip: Combine it in one loop with the Durupınar site and the Ahmed-i Hani tomb rather than driving out for the crater alone — on its own it is a hole in a field.
rev: Reviews are split between people who enjoy the oddity and people who feel cheated after a 30 km drive, and several note the site sits in a border zone where you may be asked for ID.
onward: Iğdır (IGD) airport, then Doğubayazıt and about 30 km east towards the Gürbulak border; car essential

name: Balık Gölü
desc: A cold volcanic lake at 2,250 m ringed by bare hills, stocked with trout and surrounded in summer by the black tents and flocks of families who bring animals up from the plain. There is a small island with a ruined chapel, no development to speak of, and night skies with nothing to dim them.
season: Jun–Sep only; the access road is under snow the rest of the year
tip: Bring everything you need including fuel — the handful of bungalows are basic, there is no shop, and the last 25 km of road is rough gravel.
todo: Walk the shoreline to the island view
Trout grilled at a lakeside hut
rev: Campers rate the emptiness and the fishing, while warning about the punishing access track, litter left by weekend picnickers, and nights that drop near freezing even in August.
onward: Iğdır (IGD) airport, then Doğubayazıt and roughly 60 km southwest on a partly unsurfaced road

name: Diyadin Hot Springs
desc: Water comes out of the ground here at over 70 °C and has built travertine terraces and a natural steam-filled cave you can sit in. The Murat river cuts a small canyon alongside, crossed by a slender Seljuk bridge. It is a working local spa town, not a resort — concrete pools, families, and steam rising in the cold.
season: Oct–Apr is when a scalding pool at 1,800 m makes most sense; open all year
tip: Ask for the natural cave bath rather than the hotel pools, and go early — by midday the cave fills and the queue moves slowly.
rev: Bathers rate the heat and the price, but reviews are consistent about tired facilities, poor changing rooms, litter around the travertines and strict separation of men's and women's hours.
onward: Ağrı (AJI) airport, then about 70 km east on the Doğubayazıt road; minibuses run from Ağrı

name: Van Fortress and the Old City
tr: Van Kalesi ve Eski Van Şehri
desc: A long limestone ridge above the lake, carved by the Urartians in the 9th century BC with royal rock tombs and a trilingual inscription cut by Xerxes into the cliff. Below the south side lies the flattened old city, abandoned after 1915: two ruined mosques and a minaret standing in open grass.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the ridge is exposed and there is no shade at all
tip: Climb it for sunset over the lake, then walk down into the empty old city — most visitors never realise the mound of grass below the rock is a whole vanished town.
todo: Ruined old city below the south face
rev: The lake view at dusk gets consistent praise; the complaints are a steep unshaded stair, loose railings above serious drops, and almost no interpretation of what you are looking at.
entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Van (VAN) airport, then 5 km west of the city centre; taxis wait at the base of the rock

name: Akdamar Island and Gevaş
desc: A 10th-century Armenian church on a small island in Lake Van, its outer walls carved in continuous relief — Jonah and the whale, David and Goliath, vines and animals running round the drum. Almond trees cover the island and the water is turquoise and alkaline. The ferry leaves from Gevaş on the south shore.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; boats can be cancelled in strong wind any month
tip: In Gevaş itself, walk five minutes to the Halime Hatun tomb and its Seljuk gravestone field before catching the boat — almost nobody does.
wiki: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, Aghtamar
todo: Relief carvings on the outer walls
rev: The carvings are widely called the best Armenian sculpture in Türkiye, but boats only leave when full outside peak season, waits of an hour are common, and the island gets loud with picnic groups on summer weekends.
entry: ≈€8 church · boat ≈€6 return · Museum Pass covers the church
onward: Van (VAN) airport, then 45 km west to the Gevaş jetty by dolmuş or taxi, then 20 minutes by boat
